justification: Originality is genuinely high against the two real comparators I could read. Pro Git 3.6 and the git-rebase docs both explain the mechanism in the abstract (lettered/numbered commits, no executed session); this article builds one concrete repository (a reading log), merges and rebases the *same* starting DAG from untouched branch copies, and reads every claim off real, run-code-verified `git log --graph` and `git rev-parse` output. That side-by-side-from-one-fork-point structure, plus the interactive-rebase/--autosquash worked example and the bisect --first-parent payoff, is not something either read source does. I could not get a live read of Atlassian's tutorial (JS-rendered, three fetch attempts including a text-proxy failed to return body text), so the originality claim against that specific page is not independently confirmed this round — it rests on the page's well-known shape (abstract diagrams, no scripted terminal session) rather than a fresh comparison, which is a real gap in this review, not a pass I can vouch for with the same confidence as the other two. All six primary-source quotes I checked against live pages (Pro Git's golden rule, git-rebase's 'bad idea... real fix' note and cherry-pick summary, git-merge's two-parent-commit description, git-merge-base's --is-ancestor description, git-bisect's --first-parent description, git-commit's --fixup description) are accurate and fairly bounded; the golden-rule quote uses '...' correctly to mark an elided sentence. One quote (--is-ancestor) silently changes 'Check'/'exit' to 'checks'/'exits' to fit the sentence, which is a minor unmarked edit rather than a fabrication. No filler, no restated title, no ad or consent code, no keyword stuffing; the toolchain sentence sits beside the first scripted block, not in the opening paragraph, matching the brief. Structure does not template either sibling: how-git-works ends with three stacked exercises under a named 'more experiments' heading, branching-and-merging ends with a bulleted troubleshooting list and no exercise, and this article ends on a prose paragraph about the reflog after its fourth, mid-late exercise — a third distinct shape. The four exercises are genuinely different forms: a prove-it (rule out the fast-forward case, then verify with merge-base), a predict-the-output (predict the whole-repo graph before running it, output withheld from the question), a reasoning-only exercise with no code in the prompt (what a force-push changes for a teammate), and an extend-the-code exercise (reapply the --min-parents=2 check to a third branch and explain why the same answer has a different cause). No exercise gives away its output outside the solution. Two real issues keep this well below the 8.5 bar. First, a factual self-contradiction in the 'golden rule' section: it says a rebase 'writes a new one with the same tree and a different parent,' but the article itself demonstrated the opposite two sections earlier ('Their full trees are not equal either, because annotate-for-rebase~1's tree also carries "Apr: The Fifth Season"... every tree is a complete snapshot, not a diff'). The golden-rule conclusion (old and new commits are unrelated objects) is still correct, but it is argued from a premise the page already disproved, which is exactly the kind of claim the pilot-round lessons say gets checked. Second, a reproducibility problem the same pilot-round lessons call out by name: the article pins `-b main` and `core.autocrlf false` and says that is enough to make 'the session... independent of your own init.defaultBranch setting and line-ending warnings, as in the two articles this one builds on' — but it never pins git identity or GIT_AUTHOR_DATE/GIT_COMMITTER_DATE the way how-git-works.md does, and unlike branching-and-merging.md (which never prints a raw hash, using %s%d and [...] throughout) it prints literal 40-hex-digit hashes as expected output (`git rev-parse annotate~1` / `annotate-for-rebase~1`, e.g. ac26f6b5... and e3d0a89b...). A reader typing along on their own machine, with their own name/email/clock, gets different digits there and has no warning that this block depends on settings the article did not ask them to set — the opposite of 'as in the two articles this one builds on,' since neither sibling has this gap. Both issues are writer fixes, not policy risks, and both are narrow (one paragraph, one output block) to correct.

issues.location: Section 'The golden rule, and why', paragraph beginning 'The reasoning follows directly from what this page has already shown twice over'
issues.problem: States that a rebase 'writes a new one with the same tree and a different parent.' This directly contradicts the article's own, more careful analysis two sections earlier in 'What git rebase writes instead': 'Their full trees are not equal either, because annotate-for-rebase~1's tree also carries "Apr: The Fifth Season" (it sits on top of "Add April books" now, and every tree is a complete snapshot, not a diff).' Every commit from the fork point on gets a different tree under a rebase onto a different base, not just a different parent; the golden-rule paragraph asserts the one thing the page already demonstrated is false. The ultimate conclusion (old and new commits are unrelated objects) still holds, but it is reached from a false premise, and a reader who was paying attention to the earlier section will notice the inconsistency.
issues.fixLooksLike: Replace 'writes a new one with the same tree and a different parent' with something consistent with the earlier section, e.g. 'writes a new commit whose tree and parent both differ from the original (the tree differs because it now sits on a different base, and the parent differs by construction), so the two are unrelated objects even though the edit each one carries is identical.'

issues.location: 'Same starting point, two branches' toolchain sentence, plus the 'What git rebase writes instead' block printing `git rev-parse annotate~1` / `git rev-parse annotate-for-rebase~1`
issues.problem: The toolchain sentence claims `-b main` and `core.autocrlf false` are enough to make the session reproducible, 'as in the two articles this one builds on.' But how-git-works.md additionally pins `user.name`, `user.email`, `GIT_AUTHOR_DATE` and `GIT_COMMITTER_DATE` in-article specifically because commit hashes depend on them, and branching-and-merging.md sidesteps the whole problem by never printing a raw hash (it uses `%s%d` formatting and `[...]` wildcards throughout, with an explicit note that 'commit IDs are hashes that depend on your name and clock and will differ from machine to machine'). This article does neither: it does not pin identity/date, and it prints literal, unmasked 40-hex-digit hashes ('ac26f6b58281449f4fa4079c23f7479123b68011', 'e3d0a89b599d07a1a40a1e30ca4c349833244ae4') as the expected output of `git rev-parse`. A reader following along on their own machine will get different digits there with no warning, which is exactly the failure mode the editorial brief's binding pilot-round lesson names: 'A reader's machine is not the verification harness... If an example depends on such a setting, make the article set it explicitly.'
issues.fixLooksLike: Either pin `user.name`/`user.email`/`GIT_AUTHOR_DATE`/`GIT_COMMITTER_DATE` in the opening scripted block (matching how-git-works.md) and update the toolchain sentence to say so, or drop the literal hash values from that output block (compare only the abbreviated/shape-relevant parts, or note explicitly that the two IDs will differ from the reader's own and only their inequality/equality to each other matters, as the surrounding prose already argues).

issues.location: Exercise 'Rule out the easy case first', quote of git-merge-base's --is-ancestor description
issues.problem: The live doc reads 'Check if the first <commit> is an ancestor of the second <commit>, and exit with status 0 if true, or with status 1 if not.' The article quotes it as '"checks if the first commit is an ancestor of the second, and exits with status 0 if true, or with status 1 if not"' — silently changing the imperative verbs 'Check'/'exit' to 'checks'/'exits' to fit the surrounding sentence, without brackets. The content is accurately represented; only the verb forms were altered inside quotation marks.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either quote the imperative form as written ('git-merge-base --is-ancestor, which "check[s] if the first commit is an ancestor of the second... and exit[s] with status 0..."' with brackets) or restructure the sentence so the quote can stand unedited: '... which git-merge-base documents as: "Check if the first commit is an ancestor of the second..."'.
